questions.question: In the parking lot design, why should Vehicle be an abstract class rather than a concrete class?
options: Abstract classes use less memory than concrete classes
You never instantiate a generic vehicle — you always create a specific type like Car, Bike, or Truck
Abstract classes run faster in Java and Python
It's a coding convention with no practical benefit
questions.explanation: Vehicle is abstract because you never create a generic 'Vehicle' object in the real world. You always have a specific type — Car, Bike, or Truck — each with different size requirements. This enforces type safety and lets each subclass define its own behavior.

questions.question: Which relationship best describes how ParkingLot relates to Floor in the class diagram?
options: Inheritance — Floor extends ParkingLot
Composition — ParkingLot contains Floors that cannot exist independently
Aggregation — Floors can exist without a ParkingLot
Association — they reference each other loosely
questions.explanation: ParkingLot and Floor have a composition relationship. A Floor has no meaning outside of a ParkingLot — if you destroy the ParkingLot, its Floors are destroyed too. This is the strongest form of HAS-A relationship in OOP.

questions.question: What design pattern does ParkingLot use when it provides a simple interface to manage floors, spots, and tickets?
options: Observer pattern
Facade pattern
Singleton pattern
Builder pattern
questions.explanation: The ParkingLot class acts as a Facade — it provides a simple, unified interface (park, unpark, getAvailableSpots) while hiding the complexity of coordinating floors, spots, tickets, and payment behind the scenes.

questions.question: Which SOLID principle is violated if you add EV charging logic directly inside the existing ParkingSpot class?
options: Single Responsibility Principle
Open-Closed Principle
Dependency Inversion Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
questions.explanation: The Open-Closed Principle states that classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Instead of modifying ParkingSpot, you should create an ElectricParkingSpot subclass that extends it with EV charging capabilities.

questions.question: You need to support multiple payment strategies — hourly, flat rate, and weekend pricing. Which design pattern is most appropriate?
options: Factory pattern — create different payment objects
Strategy pattern — encapsulate each pricing algorithm and swap them at runtime
Decorator pattern — wrap payments with additional fees
Template pattern — define a payment skeleton with customizable steps
questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern lets you encapsulate each pricing algorithm into its own class implementing a common PricingStrategy interface. The Ticket or PaymentService can accept any strategy at runtime, making it easy to add new pricing models without changing existing code.

questions.question: If ParkingSpot has subclasses SmallSpot, MediumSpot, and LargeSpot, what must be true for Liskov Substitution Principle to hold?
options: Each subclass must override all parent methods
Any code using ParkingSpot must work correctly with any of its subclasses without knowing the specific type
Subclasses must not add any new methods
The parent class must be declared as final
questions.explanation: Liskov Substitution Principle requires that subclasses be substitutable for their base class. If a method accepts a ParkingSpot, passing a SmallSpot, MediumSpot, or LargeSpot must not break the method's behavior or violate its contract.

questions.question: How should ParkingSpot handle the state transition from 'available' to 'occupied' to ensure thread safety when two vehicles try to park in the same spot?
options: Use a boolean flag — first thread to set it wins
Use synchronized methods or atomic compare-and-swap to ensure only one vehicle claims the spot
Let both vehicles park and resolve conflicts later
Disable concurrent access entirely with a global lock on all spots
questions.explanation: A synchronized method or atomic CAS operation ensures that only one thread can transition a spot from available to occupied. A simple boolean flag without synchronization creates a race condition where two vehicles could both see the spot as available.

questions.question: A parking lot has 5 floors with 100 spots each. Finding an available spot by iterating through all floors and spots is O(n). What data structure optimization reduces this to O(1)?
options: Use a binary search tree sorted by spot number
Maintain a min-heap or free-list per floor that tracks available spots by type
Use a hash map mapping spot ID to availability
Sort spots by availability status using merge sort on each request
questions.explanation: A min-heap or free-list per vehicle type per floor gives O(1) access to the next available spot. When a vehicle arrives, pop from the appropriate heap. When it leaves, push the spot back. This avoids scanning all 500 spots each time.

questions.question: You want to notify a display board whenever spot availability changes. Which design pattern decouples the ParkingSpot from the display board?
options: Adapter pattern
Observer pattern
Proxy pattern
Bridge pattern
questions.explanation: The Observer pattern lets ParkingSpot (or Floor) publish availability change events without knowing who listens. The DisplayBoard subscribes as an observer. This decouples the two classes — you can add more observers like a mobile app without modifying ParkingSpot.

questions.question: Should ParkingLot be a Singleton? What is the strongest argument against it?
options: Singletons are always an anti-pattern and should never be used
A company may operate multiple parking lots, and Singleton prevents creating more than one instance, reducing testability
Singletons use too much memory
Singletons cannot have methods, only static fields
questions.explanation: While a single parking lot seems natural, Singleton tightly couples code to one global instance, makes unit testing harder (can't create fresh instances), and breaks if the business expands to multiple lots. Dependency injection is a better approach.
